item.message: Skill descriptions were shortened to fit the 2% skills context budget. Codex can still see every skill, but some descriptions are shorter. Disable unused skills or plugins to leave more room for the rest.

{"brief_complete":false,"completion_reason":"Material outcome-scope decisions remain around advertised provider support, distributed routing guarantees, and mobile operator expectations.","questions":[{"decision_key":"launch_provider_support_tier","label":"Provider launch promise","context":"NexusCentral already models five cloud protocol families plus local OpenAI-compatible runtimes, but only LM Studio has live credentialed proof. “Supported” means a provider family is production-tested with real requests,",
"evidence":"`packages/contracts/index.mjs` defines OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, Google, Azure, and AWS Bedrock presets, while `docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` says cloud providers have contract-level proof only and real credentials remain unproven.","impact":"This decides which provider families the Models and Router tabs may present as production-ready, the credentials needed for acceptance, and whether NexusCentral grows through verified support tiers or promises universal compatibility immediately.","question":"Which provider-support outcome should the first production release promise?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Verified core, others preview","consequence":"Ship local runtimes plus individually credential-tested cloud families as supported; label remaining adapters preview. This keeps launch claims honest while allowing support to expand without redesign."},{"number":2,"text":"All five families supported","consequence":"Delay acceptance until every documented protocol family passes real credentialed end-to-end tests. This gives a broad launch promise but raises credential, maintenance, and regression costs."},{"number":3,"text":"Local runtimes only","consequence":"Treat cloud adapters as out of scope for production launch. This simplifies acceptance now but narrows Router value and postpones the intended provider-neutral platform outcome."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"Tiered support preserves the transport-neutral architecture while ensuring every production claim has real evidence; additional families can graduate without blocking the entire release.","priority":92},{"decision_key":"distributed_routing_launch_topology","label":"Network routing scope","context":"A “single-hop” route sends work directly from NexusCentral to one reachable provider. A “multi-hop relay” forwards work through intermediate machines when the provider is not directly reachable.","evidence":"`docs/14-PROVIDERS-AND-PEERJS-ROOMS.md` separates LAN and PeerJS transport from routing authority, while `docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` lists multi-hop relay and physical mesh scale as unproven release gaps.","impact":"This sets the production boundary for Router reliability, security testing, diagnostics, and failure recovery, and determines whether NexusCentral is initially a direct provider coordinator or a general relay network.","question":"What distributed routing topology must the first production release guarantee?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Direct single-hop only","consequence":"Support direct endpoints, directly reachable LAN providers, and direct PeerJS peers; explicitly defer relay chains. This delivers the locked provider types with a bounded trust and recovery model."},{"number":2,"text":"One trusted relay","consequence":"Allow one intermediate NexusCentral node when direct reachability fails. This expands remote use immediately but adds relay identity, authorization, evidence-transfer, and partial-failure requirements."},{"number":3,"text":"General multi-hop mesh","consequence":"Require arbitrary relay paths and physical mesh-scale proof at launch. This maximizes reach but substantially expands security, routing, observability, and acceptance scope."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"Direct single-hop routing satisfies the defined direct, LAN, and PeerJS provider scope without making the unproven relay layer part of the first production contract.","priority":87},{"decision_key":"mobile_browser_operator_scope","label":"Mobile browser outcome","context":"“Full operator parity” means a phone can author and administer everything available on desktop; “companion access” limits mobile to observing runs and acting on urgent review items.","evidence":"`docs/12-IMPLEMENTATION-STATUS.md` reports desktop and mobile Playwright proof, while `apps/web/app/page.jsx` is still the five-tab shell that must become the six-tab operator interface.","impact":"This determines responsive UX depth, which controls belong on small screens, mobile acceptance tests, and whether long-term product design treats phones as primary workstations or operational companions.","question":"What must a mobile browser let a technical operator accomplish at production launch?","choices":[{"number":1,"text":"Monitor and review","consequence":"Provide run status, evidence viewing, approval or rejection, cancellation, and essential service health on mobile; keep workflow authoring and complex Router configuration desktop-first. This supports urgent collaboration without compressing every advanced tool into a phone UI."},{"number":2,"text":"Full operator parity","consequence":"Require all six tabs and every authoring or administration workflow to be fully usable on phones. This maximizes flexibility but substantially increases interaction design and acceptance scope."},{"number":3,"text":"Read-only status","consequence":"Allow mobile users to inspect work and runs but make no state changes. This is safer and cheaper now, but weakens remote operational response and collaboration."},{"number":4,"text":"Mobile unsupported","consequence":"Make desktop-width browsers the only production web target. This minimizes launch scope but discards existing mobile proof and limits concurrent-user accessibility."}],"allow_multiple":false,"recommended_choice":1,"recommendation_reason":"Companion access covers time-sensitive operational actions while preserving a clear desktop-first technical workspace for dense authoring and configuration tasks.","priority":78}]}
